candidate_concepts.label: Compiler: Whole-Program Translator
candidate_concepts.description: A compiler translates an entire high-level language program into machine code before execution, producing an executable file.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that a compiler converts the whole program at once and saves machine code.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source defines a compiler and describes its translation process in the 'What is a Compiler?' section.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The concept is a single, self-contained teachable idea that can be assessed with a few focused questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Interpreter: Line-by-Line Executor
candidate_concepts.description: An interpreter translates and executes a high-level language program line by line, without producing a separate machine code file.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that an interpreter works one statement at a time and does not save machine code.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces the interpreter concept in the 'What is an Interpreter?' section, contrasting it with compilers.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a distinct, checkable concept that complements the compiler definition and is essential for understanding the difference.

candidate_concepts.label: Error Handling: Bulk vs Line-by-Line
candidate_concepts.description: Compilers display all errors after compiling the entire program, while interpreters show errors for each line as it is executed.
coverage_criteria: Student can contrast how compilers and interpreters report errors and the implications for debugging.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source's comparison table explicitly states error display differences: 'Errors are displayed in Compiler after Compiling together' vs 'Errors are displayed in every single line.'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The error handling distinction is a practical concept that can be verified with simple questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Speed: Compiled Faster, Interpreted Slower
candidate_concepts.description: Compiled code runs faster because the translation occurs beforehand, while interpreted code runs slower due to line-by-line translation overhead.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why compiled programs execute faster than interpreted ones.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source repeatedly states that 'Compiled codes run faster than Interpreter' and 'Interpreted codes run slower than Compiler', providing rationale.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a critical distinction that can be tested by asking for performance comparisons and reasons.

candidate_concepts.label: Optimization: Compiler Advantage
candidate_concepts.description: Compilers can optimize code because they analyze the entire program upfront, whereas interpreters have limited optimization due to line-by-line processing.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how compilers achieve better optimization and why interpreters lag.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source states in the table: 'The compiler can see code upfront which helps in running the code faster because of performing Optimization' vs 'Interpreters work by line... Optimization is slower'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is specific enough to verify via a direct question about optimization capabilities.

candidate_concepts.label: Use Environments: Production vs Development
candidate_concepts.description: Compilers are typically used in production environments for their performance, while interpreters are favored in development for easier debugging and flexibility.
coverage_criteria: Student can match compiler and interpreter to appropriate use cases and explain why.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source mentions 'The use of Compilers mostly happens in Production Environment' and 'The use of Interpreters is mostly in Programming and Development Environments' in the comparison table.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical concept that can be tested by asking which type is used where and why.

source_local_connector_candidates.reason: The source directly compares the compiler and interpreter as two different translation models, highlighting their contrasting approaches.
